This one is genuinely hard because the artwork is basically one big blue-to-white gradient, and so in that case we cannot really use a background to surface gradient to imitate it. Otherwise, there is for sure going to be some points in the gradient where the foreground cannot be distinguished from the background. So even though the artwork is very strongly a gradient, this is a rare case where we have to go flat. You can even see a case that should be forbidden, which is that the foreground and the background have the same color in option A's palette (or at least not visually distinguishable). This should give an APCA contrast of 0, which is strictly forbidden between foreground and background

Follow-up on the calibration-2 strong ({bg #000102, surface #380703, fg #d50306, accent #7e0202}, all reds): 'could also have been nice with a Slate #706c6d accent, so it's not full red'. An alternative sample, not a downgrade — the all-red palette stays strong. Evidence for a mild hue-diversity preference on the accent when fg already carries the identity hue (adjacent to the skap one-hue-one-direction principle: the two reds are one direction; a neutral accent diversifies without stealing identity).

Sharpening the Slate-accent sample: 'in this case Slate #706c6d almost acts as a true *accent* since the entire palette is red.' Principle: accent-ness is CONTEXTUAL to the palette, not absolute — the accent role is what stands apart from the palette's dominant hue field. In a monochromatic (all-red) palette a neutral is the true accent; in a neutral-heavy palette a chromatic color is. Current machinery scores accent chroma/identity absolutely; it has no notion of within-palette distinctiveness as the accent's job.

Flo, on the contextual-accent observation ('the machinery scores accent chroma and identity absolutely'): 'that's the kind of thing I meant when I said looking at the whole thing.' Framing: whole-palette relational properties are a FAMILY, not one-offs. Member 1: gamut coverage (palette vs artwork, batch-26, integrated). Member 2: contextual accent-ness (role vs rest-of-palette, candidate). The family question for any future arm: which other role qualities are relational rather than absolute (foreground separability? surface support?).

This artwork is an exception, because 
- it clearly contains a very strong blue-to-white gradient
- it *only* contains blue and white
because of its limited "range" of hues, using a gradient as a background guarantees that both colors are used in the background (white and blue) and that the foreground colors (foreground and accent) will be almost impossible to distinguish in *at least some parts* of the gradient.

There is technically a way to represent both: limit the background gradient to only a portion of the full range (for example deep blue Nazar to light blue Skinny Jeans) and then use the rest of the range for the foreground and accent. I did an example of this in "One palette you'd endorse" below.
